lessons.title: Common Diseases and Parasites
lessons.body: Grasscutters are hardy, but they still get sick. The most common diseases you will see are coccidiosis, mange, pneumonia, and intestinal worms. Coccidiosis is caused by a tiny parasite in the gut. It mostly hits young grasscutters, causing bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, and death if not treated. You will see them sitting hunched with rough fur. Treat with amprolium or sulphonamides in drinking water for 5 days. Mange is caused by mites that burrow into the skin. You will notice hair loss, crusty patches on the ears, nose, and feet, and the animal scratching constantly. Treat by injecting ivermectin (0.2 mg per kg body weight) under the skin, and repeat after 10 days. Also clean the cage with a flame or strong disinfectant to kill mites. Pneumonia is common when the hutch is damp or poorly ventilated. Signs include coughing, noisy breathing, and a runny nose. Keep the hutch dry and use antibiotics like oxytetracycline if severe. Intestinal worms are very common in grasscutters that eat fresh grass. You may see worms in droppings or a pot-bellied look. Deworm every 3 months with albendazole or levamisole. External parasites like ticks and fleas can also attack. Use tick grease or spray the hutch with acaricide. Always isolate sick animals immediately to stop spread. Many diseases come from dirty water, wet bedding, or introducing new animals without quarantine. Prevention is cheaper than treatment: clean cages daily, provide clean water, and avoid overcrowding. If you see sudden deaths, take the dead animal to a vet for post-mortem to know the real cause.

lessons.title: Signs of Illness and Early Detection
lessons.body: Catching sickness early saves money and animals. You must check your grasscutters at least twice a day, morning and evening. Look for changes in behaviour, eating, and droppings. A healthy grasscutter is alert, moves quickly, has bright eyes, and eats well. A sick one may sit in a corner, ignore food, and have dull or half-closed eyes. One of the first signs is loss of appetite. If an animal does not finish its feed by evening, separate it and watch closely. Check the droppings: normal droppings are firm, dark, and pellet-shaped. Diarrhoea or bloody droppings mean a gut problem. Hard, dry droppings mean constipation or dehydration. Listen for coughing, sneezing, or noisy breathing â these point to respiratory disease. Look at the fur: rough, dull, or patchy fur means mites, worms, or poor nutrition. Check the eyes and nose for discharge. A healthy grasscutter has no discharge. Feel the belly: if it is bloated or hard, there may be worms or gas. Check the feet for sores or swelling â these can become infected. Also watch for sudden weight loss: weigh your breeding stock monthly using a hanging scale. A drop of more than 10% in a month is a red flag. Other signs include head tilting, circling, or paralysis â these suggest nervous system problems and need a vet immediately. Keep a simple record book for each cage: note any change, date, and action taken. Early detection means you can treat with simple drugs before the whole herd is sick. If you see more than two animals sick at once, call a vet or extension officer the same day.

lessons.title: Vaccination and Deworming Programs
lessons.body: Grasscutters do not have many commercial vaccines, but you can follow a simple deworming and health schedule. Deworming is the most important routine treatment. Use albendazole (10 mg per kg body weight) or levamisole (7.5 mg per kg) every 3 months. For a 2 kg grasscutter, that is 20 mg albendazole â usually 1 ml of a 2.5% suspension. Give orally using a syringe without a needle. Mark the date on your calendar. If you have many animals, deworm them all on the same day. Treat new animals before they join the main herd. For external parasites, use ivermectin injection (0.2 mg per kg) every 6 months, or apply tick grease to ears and feet monthly. Coccidiosis is common in young ones â you can use amprolium in water for 5 days as a preventive during weaning (around 4-6 weeks old). There is no routine vaccine for grasscutters in most African countries, but you can vaccinate against pasteurellosis if your vet recommends it and the vaccine is available. Some farmers use fowl typhoid vaccine off-label, but do not do this without veterinary advice. Always keep a record: date, drug, dose, and animal ID. Withdraw meat from animals treated with drugs for the recommended period (usually 7-14 days) before slaughter. Deworming works best when combined with clean management. If you deworm but keep animals on dirty floors, they get reinfected fast. So deworm and clean the same week. For pregnant females, use only safe dewormers like albendazole â avoid levamisole in early pregnancy. For young ones under 8 weeks, use half dose. Store drugs in a cool, dark place, away from children. Check expiry dates â expired drugs do not work. If you cannot afford dewormers, use natural options like papaya seeds (2-3 seeds per kg body weight) but they are less effective. Always consult a vet or experienced farmer before starting any vaccination program.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures
lessons.body: Biosecurity means keeping diseases out of your farm. It is the cheapest and most effective health tool. Start with a fence around your grasscutter house. No visitor should enter without permission. Keep a footbath at the entrance with disinfectant (e.g., 2% caustic soda or 1% formalin). Change the disinfectant every 3 days. Wear dedicated boots and overalls inside the farm â do not wear them outside. When you return from the market or another farm, do not enter your grasscutter house immediately. Shower and change clothes first. Quarantine all new animals for at least 30 days in a separate cage far from the main herd. Watch them for signs of illness. Test for parasites by taking a stool sample to a vet. Only mix them after quarantine. Control rats, mice, and wild birds â they carry diseases and parasites. Use traps and keep feed in sealed containers. Do not keep chickens, ducks, or pigs near grasscutters â they can share diseases. Clean and disinfect cages weekly. Remove old bedding and droppings daily. Use a flame torch to burn mite eggs on wooden cages. Provide clean, chlorinated water (1 teaspoon of bleach per 20 litres) â let it stand 30 minutes before giving. Store feed off the floor on pallets. Never feed mouldy or spoiled feed. If an animal dies, bury it deep (1 metre) or burn it â never throw it in the bush. Keep a record of all visitors and any new animals. If you see sick animals, isolate them immediately and treat. Do not share tools or equipment with other farms. If you must lend, disinfect before and after. Train your family members on these rules. A simple sign at the gate: âNo entry without permission â biosecurity area.â These steps cost little but save you from losing your whole herd.

lessons.title: First Aid and Basic Treatments
lessons.body: First aid saves lives before the vet arrives. Keep a simple first aid kit: syringes (1ml, 5ml), needles, cotton wool, iodine, hydrogen peroxide, antibiotic powder, bandages, scissors, and a thermometer. For cuts and wounds: clean with clean water and hydrogen peroxide, apply iodine, and cover with a bandage if needed. If bleeding, press with clean cloth for 5 minutes. For diarrhoea: isolate the animal, give oral rehydration solution (1 litre clean water + 1 teaspoon salt + 6 teaspoons sugar) using a syringe without needle, 5ml every 2 hours. If bloody, start amprolium in water. For mange: inject ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg) under the skin, and apply petroleum jelly mixed with sulphur to affected areas daily for 7 days. For pneumonia: keep animal warm, give oxytetracycline injection (20 mg/kg) once daily for 3 days. For worms: give albendazole orally (10 mg/kg) â repeat after 14 days. For constipation: give 2ml vegetable oil orally. For heat stress: move animal to shade, provide cool water, and wet the ears and feet. For fractures: immobilise with a splint made from a stick and bandage, then take to vet. For poisoning (e.g., from sprayed grass): give activated charcoal (1g per kg) mixed in water, and rush to vet. Never give human drugs like paracetamol or aspirin â they are toxic to grasscutters. Always weigh the animal first to calculate correct dose. Use a 5ml syringe for oral liquids, and 1ml syringe for injections. For injections, use the back of the neck or thigh muscle. Clean the site with iodine before injecting. If you are not sure, call a vet or experienced farmer. Keep records of treatment: date, drug, dose, and response. After treatment, observe for 3 days. If no improvement, change treatment or call vet. Do not reuse needles without sterilising by boiling for 20 minutes. Proper first aid reduces suffering and saves money.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians
lessons.body: A good veterinarian is your best partner in grasscutter farming. Many vets do not know much about grasscutters, so you must find one who is willing to learn with you. Start by asking your local veterinary office or extension officer for a vet who handles small livestock or wildlife. When you call, explain that you keep grasscutters and need help with disease diagnosis and treatment. Invite the vet to visit your farm at least once a year for a general check-up. During the visit, show your records and ask for advice on deworming, vaccination, and biosecurity. If an animal dies suddenly, take the fresh carcass to the vet for post-mortem â this reveals the real cause. For laboratory tests, collect stool samples in a clean bottle and label with date and animal ID. The vet can test for worms, coccidia, and bacteria. When the vet prescribes drugs, ask for the exact dose, route, and withdrawal period. Write it down. Do not guess. If the vet is far, use mobile phone consultations â send clear photos of sick animals and their droppings. Many vets now offer telemedicine. Pay the vet fairly â it is cheaper than losing animals. You can also join a farmer group and share the cost of a vet visit. If no vet is available, contact your national veterinary research institute or agricultural university â they often help farmers. Always follow the vetâs instructions exactly. If the animal does not improve after 3 days, call back. Keep a vet record book: date, problem, treatment, and outcome. This helps the vet learn about grasscutters too. Remember: vets can also help you get permits to sell meat legally. Build a good relationship â invite the vet to see your healthy animals as well. A vet who knows your farm will respond faster in an emergency. Never use drugs without veterinary advice, especially antibiotics â misuse creates resistance. With a vet on your team, your grasscutter business is safer and more profitable.

quiz.q: Which disease causes bloody diarrhoea in young grasscutters?
quiz.explanation: Coccidiosis is a gut parasite that typically causes bloody diarrhoea, especially in young animals.

quiz.q: What is the recommended treatment for mange in grasscutters?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin injected under the skin at 0.2 mg/kg is effective against mites causing mange.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm grasscutters with albendazole?
quiz.explanation: A routine deworming schedule of every 3 months is recommended to control intestinal worms.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests a grasscutter may have pneumonia?
quiz.explanation: Pneumonia causes respiratory signs like coughing and noisy breathing.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do when you see a sick grasscutter?
quiz.explanation: Isolating a sick animal prevents the spread of disease to healthy ones.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of illness in a grasscutter?
quiz.explanation: Rough, dull fur is a common sign of illness such as parasites or poor nutrition.

quiz.q: How often should you check your grasscutters for signs of illness?
options: D) Only when they look sick
quiz.explanation: Checking morning and evening helps detect problems early.

quiz.q: What do hard, dry droppings in a grasscutter indicate?
quiz.explanation: Hard, dry droppings are a sign of constipation or dehydration.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to weigh grasscutters for accurate dosing?
quiz.explanation: A hanging scale gives the body weight needed to calculate drug doses.

quiz.q: What should you do if more than two animals are sick at once?
quiz.explanation: Multiple sick animals suggest a serious outbreak; a vet should be called the same day.

quiz.q: What is the dose of albendazole for a 2 kg grasscutter?
quiz.explanation: Albendazole is given at 10 mg per kg body weight, so 2 kg requires 20 mg.

quiz.q: Which drug is used to treat coccidiosis?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium in drinking water for 5 days is a standard treatment for coccidiosis.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat ivermectin injection for mange?
quiz.explanation: A second ivermectin injection after 10 days kills newly hatched mites.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for meat after deworming?
quiz.explanation: Most dewormers require a withdrawal period of 7-14 days before slaughter.

quiz.q: Which dewormer should be avoided in early pregnancy?
quiz.explanation: Levamisole can cause abortion in early pregnancy; albendazole is safer.

quiz.q: What is the correct dose of ivermectin for external parasites?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin is injected at 0.2 mg per kg body weight for mites and ticks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a footbath at the farm entrance?
quiz.explanation: A footbath with disinfectant kills germs on boots before entering the farm.

quiz.q: How long should new grasscutters be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: A 30-day quarantine allows time for any disease to show before mixing with the herd.

quiz.q: Which animals should be kept away from grasscutters to prevent disease spread?
quiz.explanation: Chickens and pigs can carry diseases that may infect grasscutters.

quiz.q: How often should you change disinfectant in the footbath?
quiz.explanation: Disinfectant loses potency; changing it every 3 days keeps it effective.

quiz.q: What should you do with a dead grasscutter?
quiz.explanation: Burying deep or burning prevents disease spread from carcasses.

quiz.q: What is the correct oral rehydration solution for diarrhoea?
options: A) 1L water + 1 tsp salt + 6 tsp sugar
quiz.explanation: This mixture replaces lost electrolytes and fluids in sick animals.

quiz.q: Which human drug is toxic to grasscutters?
quiz.explanation: Paracetamol and aspirin are toxic to grasscutters and should never be used.

quiz.q: How should you give an injection to a grasscutter?
options: B) In the back of the neck or thigh
quiz.explanation: The back of the neck or thigh muscle is the safest site for injections.

quiz.q: What is the first aid for a bleeding wound?
options: B) Press with clean cloth for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Direct pressure for 5 minutes stops bleeding before cleaning and dressing.

quiz.q: How often should you sterilise reusable needles?
quiz.explanation: Needles must be boiled for 20 minutes after each use to prevent infection.

quiz.q: What is the role of a veterinarian in grasscutter farming?
quiz.explanation: Vets diagnose illnesses, prescribe treatments, and advise on health programs.

quiz.q: What should you do before a vet visit?
options: D) Clean the farm with bleach
quiz.explanation: Having records and stool samples ready helps the vet make a quick diagnosis.

quiz.q: How can you consult a vet if they are far away?
options: B) Wait for them to visit
quiz.explanation: Mobile phone consultations with clear photos are a useful alternative when vets are distant.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using antibiotics without veterinary advice?
quiz.explanation: Misuse of antibiotics leads to drug resistance, making future treatments ineffective.
